title: Merge Lightest Neighbors Until Sorted
statement:
You get an integer array nums. While the array is not in non-decreasing order, perform this step:

  • Among all pairs of neighbouring elements, find the pair with the smallest sum. If several pairs share that sum, take the leftmost one.
  • Replace the two elements with a single element equal to their sum. The array gets one shorter.

Return how many steps are performed. An array that is already non-decreasing needs 0 steps. A one-element array is always sorted.

examples.why: The lightest pair is (1, 3), not the out-of-order (3, 2): [4, 4, 2]. Then (4, 2) gives [4, 6], which is sorted.
→ [4, 3, 2, 4] → [4, 5, 4]. Now both pairs sum to 9 and the leftmost wins: [9, 4] → [13]. Picking the right pair would have stopped at [4, 9] after 3 steps.
Equal neighbours are allowed; the array is already non-decreasing.

hints: The rule is fully specified, so this is a simulation. What does one step cost on a plain array?
Each step: scan for the leftmost minimum-sum pair (use strict < so earlier pairs win ties), splice the pair into one element, and recheck whether the array is sorted.
To go faster, keep the elements in a linked list, pairs in a min-heap keyed by (sum, left position), and a running count of out-of-order neighbours. Stop when that count is 0.

explain.intuition:
There is no choice to optimise: the rule decides every step. The job is to simulate it exactly. Two details decide correctness: the pair chosen is the one with the smallest sum, not one that is out of order, and ties go to the leftmost pair. The second example shows a tie that changes the answer.

A direct simulation scans all pairs per step and is O(n²) overall, fine for this size. For a faster version, store elements in a doubly linked list so a merge is O(1), keep every live pair in a min-heap ordered by sum then by left position, and keep a counter of descents (a[i] > a[i+1]). A merge only changes the descents around the merged spot, so the counter updates in O(1). Heap entries that no longer match the list are skipped when popped.
steps: If the array is already non-decreasing, return 0.
Find the index i of the leftmost pair with the smallest nums[i] + nums[i+1].
Replace the pair with its sum and count one step.
Repeat until the array is non-decreasing, then return the count.
pitfalls: Merging an out-of-order pair instead of the lightest pair. In [4, 1, 3, 2] the first merge is (1, 3).
Using <= while scanning, which picks the rightmost of tied pairs.
Treating equal neighbours as unsorted. Non-decreasing allows 2, 2.

complexity.time: O(n²) simulation; O(n log n) with list + heap

solutions.title: Direct simulation
solutions.idea: Scan for the leftmost lightest pair, splice it, and repeat while the array is unsorted.

solutions.title: Linked list + heap + descent counter
solutions.idea: Merges are O(1) in a linked list; a heap keyed by (sum, left index) finds the next pair; a counter of descents says when to stop. Stale heap entries are skipped.

followups: The array can have 100 000 elements. Which parts of the direct simulation become the bottleneck, and how does the heap version avoid them?
Why is a stale heap entry safe to skip, and why is an entry whose sum still matches safe to use?
